name: Solanthex
description: Solanthex is a long-duration hedonic baseline stabilizer that produces a sustained, gentle sense of satisfaction and well-being without euphoria or cognitive impairment. It works by modulating the brain's default sense of sufficiency — the background feeling of whether what one has is enough. Lazarus markets it as a treatment for chronic dissatisfaction disorder, existential anxiety, and quality-of-life deficit syndrome, all diagnostic categories that critics note Lazarus itself helped define.
effects: Sustained low-level sense of contentment and sufficiency
Decreased desire for change in circumstances
Reduced envy, status anxiety, and upward social comparison
side_effects: Reduction in drive to improve one's actual circumstances
Users may accept objectively poor conditions with inappropriate equanimity
Subtle blunting of aspiration and goal formation
Long-term users report difficulty feeling excited about genuinely good things
Social critics note the drug makes inequality more tolerable without addressing it
Cessation after long-term use produces acute dissatisfaction and existential distress
cultural_context: Solanthex is the most politically controversial legal drug in GLMZ. In Tier 4 and 5, it is used for genuine quality-of-life management — high-stress executives and anxious Spire residents use it to enjoy what they have. In Tier 1 and 2, it is prescribed at extraordinary rates, and critics argue it is a chemical mechanism of social control — a drug that makes people on the Shelf feel okay about being on the Shelf. Lazarus's response is that the drug treats a real condition and that suffering is not politically useful. The debate continues.
story_hooks: A Shelf neighborhood that was becoming politically organized suddenly shows a dramatic uptick in Solanthex prescriptions from a Lazarus-affiliated clinic — someone is trying to chemically demobilize a movement
A Spire journalist goes on Solanthex for a month to write a piece about it and realizes, three weeks in, that they have lost the ambition to finish the article

A Lazarus whistleblower reveals that the diagnostic criteria for chronic dissatisfaction disorder were written to include essentially any expression of political or economic grievance — the drug was always a pacification tool
